title: Five Leadership Traits Every Leader Can Learn From Sonoco Military Veterans
summary: Continuous improvement applies to more than manufacturing processes at Sonoco. It’s the mindset of an effective leader.
body_markdown:
In recognition of Veterans Day, Sonoco Senior Environmental Engineer and Marine Corps veteran, Jim Lee, and Sonoco Operational Excellence Practitioner and Army veteran, Kevin Moore, shared more about what leadership means to them and five key military leadership traits that every leader should work to develop.


### **A Leader Communicates With Tact**


Sonoco Senior Environmental Engineer & Marine Corps veteran, Jim Lee


“Tact is not avoiding difficult conversations but knowing how to have them,” stated Lee. “A tactful leader can deliver difficult feedback, hold people accountable and disagree with others. What distinguishes them is their approach to communication.”


An effective leader knows that tactful communication is honest, respectful and purposeful. Lee shared, “If a leader embarrasses someone during a meeting, they’ve technically delivered the message but damaged trust and probably made future communication difficult.”


A tactful leader works to say things the right way and achieve their goals by first asking themselves:


- What does this person need to hear?
- How do they need to hear it?
- What am I trying to achieve?


“Employees are observing leaders to see how they react,” said Lee. “By holding others accountable and preserving everyone’s dignity, a leader can drive results in a respectful manner.”


### **A Leader Acts With Integrity**


“Integrity is what happens when nobody is watching and when doing the right thing becomes a personal inconvenience,” shared Lee. Team members constantly observe a leader’s behavior and notice patterns like:


- When a leader takes responsibility
- What habits and qualities a leader models
- To whom a leader gives credit
- What actions a leader rewards
- If a leader applies the rules equally
- How a leader’s words and actions match
- What behavior a leader tolerates


Lee stated, “A common test of integrity happens when things don’t go well. They can make the situation sound better than it is or tell the truth. Teams often forgive mistakes, but they rarely forgive dishonesty.”


A leader who tells the truth and creates a safe environment for people to report bad news enables the organization to make good decisions going forward. Lee said, “Is your team comfortable telling you something is going wrong?”


### **A Leader Demonstrates Enthusiasm**


“Enthusiasm displays sincere interest and optimism,” said Lee. “It’s not fake cheerfulness or pretending everything is going well but acknowledging problems and communicating how a team can work together to resolve them.”


When a leader walks into a difficult situation with a negative attitude or mindset, that attitude quickly spreads to his team. “Having the right attitude and bringing the right energy to the table changes performance,” explains Lee.


Lee shared an example of how two leaders facing the same challenge can approach it differently:


- Approach 1: “Leadership dumped another impossible deadline on us. Let’s just get through it.”
- Approach 2: “We have a challenging deadline. Here’s what we’re facing, our plan and where each of you can make a difference.”


“Giving the team a reason to believe they can succeed is leadership,” said Lee. “We don’t always have control over circumstances, but we can influence how people experience those circumstances.”


### **A Leader Remains Composed**


Sonoco Operational Excellence Practitioner & Army veteran, Kevin Moore


“How you carry yourself when things aren’t going well speaks loudly to the people around you,” shared Moore. “A leader who remains composed in their appearance, professionalism and conduct demonstrates confidence in themselves and their ability to lead.”


A leader’s reaction can either stabilize a challenging situation or make it worse. Moore said, “When a team misses a project deadline, the team doesn’t expect a leader to fix everything in five minutes, but they do want evidence that someone is composed.” These cues often look like:


- Remaining calm
- Willing to own the situation
- Talking to the stakeholders
- Protecting the team from blame-shifting
- Looking at the fire in front of them and the whole picture


“Leadership is revealed when everything goes wrong. In the middle of failure, people look to the leader’s reaction to see if they are in good hands,” shares Moore.


### **A Leader Serves Unselfishly**


“An effective leader understands that leadership is about service, not status,” said Moore. “An unselfish leader develops people, shares credit, accepts responsibility, mentors others, removes obstacles and makes decisions for the good of the team.”


When a project succeeds, a leader reveals their character through the people they choose to recognize. A self-focused leader makes themselves the hero of the story, but an unselfish leader deliberately shines the spotlight on specific people and contributions that enabled the team to win.


> As Moore and Lee stated, “Most people work hard for a paycheck. They’ll do what’s required to hit targets and deliver the basics, but people go above and beyond for leaders who make them feel genuinely valued.”


Leaders who create a culture where people want to contribute turn employees into true partners. “If a leader wants team members to be invested, they give away the credit in public and own the responsibility in private,” Moore shared.


### **Putting Leadership to the Test**


At Sonoco, one of our key values is treating people with respect—how we would want to be treated. When things go wrong, a leader acts respectfully by carefully reflecting and asking:


- How should I communicate this message?
- What is the truth?
- What energy am I bringing?
- How am I responding to this pressure?
- What does my team need from me?
